titre: The Lamp Base That Remains a Work of Art
accroche: In 1954, the Supreme Court rules that a statuette sold as a lamp base remains protected by copyright: form is not the same thing as use.
contenu_vulgarise:
Some partners make and sell electric lamps. One of them sculpts statuettes of male and female dancers using the traditional clay-model technique; a production mold makes it possible to cast copies in semivitreous porcelain. They are first sold mounted as lamps, wired and fitted with a socket and a shade. Only afterward do the Steins submit the statuettes alone, without lamp parts, to the U.S. Copyright Office for registration as “works of art,” and obtain their certificates. The statuettes then sell in large numbers across the country, both as lamp bases and as statuettes. Other partners, the Mazers, who are also lamp manufacturers, copy the statuettes without authorization, mount them as lamps, and sell them. The Steins sue them in Maryland.

## A utilitarian object can remain a work of art

The Mazers attack the very validity of the Steins' copyright: the statuettes were published as lamps before being registered, and having them registered after the fact as works of art would, they say, be an abusive use of copyright, one that would invalidate the registration. The district court dismisses the Steins' complaint, thereby siding with the Mazers. The Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals reverses and holds the copyrights valid. The Mazers then take the case to the Supreme Court.

On March 8, 1954, in an opinion by Justice Stanley Reed, the Court affirms. Nothing in the copyright statute, or in any other, forbids a thing from being both patentable and copyrighted: “Neither the Copyright Statute nor any other says that because a thing is patentable it may not be copyrighted.” It does not even rule on whether the statuettes are patentable. It distinguishes what each right protects: unlike a patent, copyright gives no exclusive right to the art described; it protects the expression, here the sculpted form, and not the mechanical or utilitarian aspects. That the statuette is later used to manufacture lamps in series does not strip it of this protection: the Court finds nothing in the law that would support the argument that industrial exploitation of a work bars or invalidates its registration.

The protection has a limit, which the Court spells out: without copying, there is no infringement. The Steins can bar the copying of their statuettes, but not the use by others of similar dancer figures in lamps. The Mazers remain free to make lamps; what they are charged with is having copied the statuettes themselves.

## A form that can be detached from its function

The Court does not yet speak of separability. The U.S. Congress would take up the solution of Mazer in the Copyright Act of 1976, under that name: an aesthetic form can be protected even when it adorns a useful object. Judges then remained divided for a long time over how to test whether a feature truly separates from the object. The Supreme Court finally set a test on March 22, 2017, in Star Athletica v. Varsity Brands, concerning the lines, chevrons, and colored shapes on the surface of cheerleader uniforms, relying on the 1976 Act and on Mazer.

The dividing line between art and use, first drawn over a lamp base, thus waited sixty-three years for the test the Supreme Court chose to settle it.

citation.texte: Neither the Copyright Statute nor any other says that because a thing is patentable it may not be copyrighted.
citation.source: Mazer v. Stein, 347 U.S. 201, opinion of the Court, March 8, 1954

carte.punch: A statuette sold as a lamp base remains, in its form, a work of art.
carte.idee: In 1954, the Supreme Court rules that statuettes of dancers, first sold mounted as lamps and then registered as works of art, remain protected by copyright. Sculpted form and utilitarian use are not mutually exclusive: only the form is protected, never the function.

quiz.question: Why does the Supreme Court rule in 1954 that the Steins' statuettes remain protected by copyright despite their use as lamp bases?
choix: Because copyright protects the sculpted form itself, regardless of the industrial use later made of it
Because the Steins had also filed a patent on the lamp's electrical mechanism, which covered the whole object
Because the Mazers had copied only part of the statuette, not enough to constitute infringement
Because the law at the time prohibited any mass production of an object already registered as a work of art
quiz.explication: The Court holds that copyright protects the sculpted form, not its mechanical or utilitarian aspects, and that industrial use of the statuette does not take that protection away; an object can be patentable and protected by copyright, the two not being mutually exclusive. The other three answers are wrong: the Court does not even rule on the statuettes' patentability, it notes that the Mazers copied the statuettes themselves, and nothing in the law it cites forbids a registered work from being exploited in series.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did the dispute between the Steins and the Mazers unfold before reaching the Supreme Court?
choix: The district court dismissed the Steins' complaint, then the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals held their copyrights valid
The district court sided with the Steins, later affirmed by the court of appeals
Both lower courts sided with the Mazers, which the Supreme Court affirms
The case went straight from registration at the Copyright Office to the Supreme Court
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The district court first dismisses the Steins' complaint, thereby siding with the Mazers; the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals reverses that judgment and holds the Steins' copyrights valid.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the Supreme Court, what can the Steins prevent, and what can they not prevent?
choix: They can prevent the Mazers from making any lamps, even without copying the statuettes
They can bar the copying of their statuettes, but not the use by others of similar dancer figures
They can forbid anyone, including themselves, from using their statuettes industrially
They can prevent nothing, since copyright does not apply to objects sold as lamp bases
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Court makes clear that without copying there is no infringement: the Steins can bar the copying of their statuettes, but not the use by others of similar dancer figures in lamps.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many years passed between Mazer v. Stein (1954) and Star Athletica v. Varsity Brands (2017), the decision that sets the separability test?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Supreme Court sets the separability test only in 2017, in Star Athletica, sixty-three years after drawing the distinction between form and use in Mazer v. Stein in 1954.
